video_title: Brookfield’s Connor Teskey on the Real Bottleneck in the AI Buildout
gist: Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey (~$1.3T AUM) argues the AI buildout's bottleneck is execution capability (land, grid connection, power, operations), not capital or demand, and that power demand so exceeds supply that even a demand decline would leave a large imbalance. He also covers sovereign AI as Europe's demand driver, energy storage as Brookfield's fastest-growing energy segment, the Oaktree build-vs-buy logic, and alternatives growth driven by the under-penetrated (<=2%) individual investor market.

insights.claim: Connor Teskey says the scarce input in the AI infrastructure buildout is neither capital nor demand but the ability to deliver projects: land development, grid connection, power supply, building and operating large-scale facilities, and redundancy.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Value accrues to operators with both capital and operating capability, not just financiers.

insights.claim: Teskey argues market fears that AI infrastructure demand is fragile, triggered by more efficient models or a hyperscaler dropping a data center lease, are divorced from fundamentals because supply is only a small fraction of demand.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Selloffs on efficiency or lease-cancellation headlines may be buying opportunities in AI infra/power.

insights.claim: Teskey claims that even if AI and energy demand growth slowed, plateaued or declined, there would still be a huge supply-demand imbalance favoring providers of power and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Pricing power for power/infra providers is robust to demand downside scenarios.

insights.claim: Teskey calls the energy and infrastructure capital need perhaps the greatest in history and expects the theme to last through the end of this decade and beyond, with very attractive returns.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Multi-year deployment runway for infra-focused alternative managers.

insights.claim: Within roughly four or five years, electricity went from something taken for granted to the single biggest bottleneck to growth for the largest companies and countries, according to Teskey.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Power access is now a strategic constraint for hyperscalers and nations.

themes.theme: US corporate demand vs. European sovereign AI

insights.claim: Teskey says US AI infrastructure demand is driven organically by the hyperscalers, since most of the world's 15 largest technology companies are American, while Europe lacks that homegrown corporate demand base.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Different demand origins imply different counterparty risk by region.

insights.claim: Brookfield has signed sovereign AI agreements in France, Sweden and Qatar in which the initial off-taker supporting the AI infrastructure buildout is a sovereign rather than a hyperscaler.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Sovereign off-take is an under-appreciated, government-backstopped demand source outside the US.

insights.claim: Teskey argues nation-states are backstopping AI buildouts because they view AI as a productivity tool and do not want their populations left behind, a demand driver he sees mostly outside the US and Asia-Pacific.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Expect more government-anchored data center deals in Europe and the Middle East.

insights.claim: Teskey dates the electricity supply-demand imbalance to the late 2010s, driven by reindustrialization and electrification rather than AI, with AI later exaggerating an imbalance that already implied decades of demand growth.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Power demand thesis does not hinge on AI alone.

insights.claim: Energy storage and batteries are currently the fastest-growing segment of Brookfield's energy business, which was not true five years ago, as storage offsets renewables' intermittency.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Storage is becoming the key complement to low-cost renewables.

insights.claim: Teskey says power buyers now demand electricity of a specific shape, location, source and duration rather than undifferentiated electrons, increasing product sophistication in power contracting.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Providers able to tailor firm, shaped power can capture premiums.

insights.claim: Large electricity users such as hyperscalers increasingly concentrate purchases among a small number of scale providers that can deliver on time and on budget, rather than choosing the lowest-cost supplier among many small developers.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Scale and delivery credibility are competitive moats; small developers lose share.

insights.claim: Ten years ago Brookfield sold power mainly to utilities and governments; today it sells the majority of its power directly to corporates, increasingly via global-scale framework agreements.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Corporate PPAs have replaced utilities as the core offtake channel.

insights.claim: Teskey says Brookfield never accepts one basis point of return discount for the decarbonization impact of an investment and does not take technology bets; its renewables case has always been commercial.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Renewables thesis rests on economics and energy security, not climate premium.

themes.theme: Build vs. buy and the Oaktree deal

insights.claim: Brookfield generally prefers to build new strategies in-house because it is cheaper and can be built exactly as desired, buying only when capabilities would be too difficult or slow to replicate, as with credit via Oaktree in 2019.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: M&A by Brookfield signals a market it considers large and time-sensitive.

insights.claim: The Oaktree deal originated when Teskey's team, tracking public alternative asset managers, judged in early 2018 that Oaktree was mispriced relative to its franchise quality; Bruce Flatt pushed for a strategic deal, leading to a privatization partnered with founders about a year later.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Illustrates Brookfield's opportunistic, partnership-style M&A approach.

insights.claim: Teskey says Brookfield viewed credit as becoming a core pillar of private markets, which justified acquiring Oaktree rather than spending 10-15 years building a credit franchise; Brookfield now owns Oaktree fully.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Private credit is central to funding the infrastructure buildout.

themes.theme: Alternatives growth from the individual market

insights.claim: Teskey estimates institutional investors allocate in the mid-teens percent to alternatives, likely rising to 20-30% over time, while the individual market (private wealth, annuities, 401k) is at 2% or less today.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Retail/wealth channel is the major incremental AUM growth lever for alt managers.

insights.claim: Teskey finds it very tough to see a scenario where allocations to alternatives slow in either the individual or institutional market, citing return premium, stability versus increasingly volatile public markets, diversification and access to companies staying private longer.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for listed alt managers' fundraising.

insights.claim: Teskey argues private capital suits large infrastructure projects that are non-income producing for two to five years of construction and then generate cash for decades, a profile that fits poorly with quarterly public-market reporting.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Infra buildout naturally shifts toward private funding.

themes.theme: Brookfield operating model and investing style

insights.claim: Brookfield sources, executes and operates in a decentralized way through dedicated local teams for each region and asset class, but allocates capital through a centralized investment committee to direct money to the best risk-adjusted returns globally.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Combines local edge with global capital allocation discipline.

insights.claim: Teskey says Brookfield invests when enough variables are in its control to produce a downside-protected, upside-asymmetric return profile, warning that demanding certainty on every variable yields a perfect track record but no investments.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Investment process tolerates residual risk where it controls key drivers.

insights.claim: Teskey says betting on being smarter than everyone forever is silly; Brookfield instead focuses on structural, enduring competitive advantages that enable attractive risk-adjusted returns at scale.
insights.speaker: Connor Teskey
insights.so_what: Moat comes from scale and operating capability, not stock-picking alpha.
